UDLCO CRH: Intuitive continuity and stewardship of multidimensional human journeys into academic flatlands: JECP onco paper draft 2 continues

 

Introduction


The manuscript investigates the epistemology and ontology of longitudinal patient journeys within healthcare systems. The primary problem addressed is that current medical architectures privilege episodic, static encounters over long-term, continuous clinical trajectories. This creates a systemic gap where vital contextual, intuitive, and highly distributed human observations are lost. The study aims to expand existing Research Questions (RQs) around observability, continuity, technology, and patient stewardship by introducing "intuition" and "anticipatory recognition" as legitimate, operationalized components of a memory-native health system.


Check out part 1 of this paper here: https://medicinedepartment.blogspot.com/2026/06/udlco-crh-first-draft-of-patient-events.html?m=1






Methods

The study utilizes a qualitative and conceptual framework analysis built upon structured clinical case reflections (e.g., "Case 1") and collaborative, cross-disciplinary scholarly dialogue. Researchers examined four core architectural axes:



  • RQ1: Observability and Journey Knowledge

  • RQ2: Continuity, Stewardship, and Longitudinal Recognition

  • RQ3: Technology, Memory, and Longitudinal Infrastructure

  • RQ4: Distributed Stewardship, Patient Participation, and Human Memory

The methodology treats clinical texts, transcripts, and practitioners' lived experiences as epistemic artifacts to deconstruct how tacit human wisdom converts into formal medical data.

Results

The analysis yielded a multi-layered framework revealing that human academic and clinical processes operate as mechanisms for capturing multidimensional, intuitive data:

  • Operationalizing Intuition: Intuition is redefined not as mysticism, but as compressed longitudinal pattern recognition that exceeds immediate articulation ($\text{Recognition} \rightarrow \text{Explanation} \rightarrow \text{Diagnosis}$).

  • Human as Infrastructure: Much of healthcare's actual continuity currently resides within human carriers (experienced clinicians, patients, and families) who act as living continuity infrastructures.

  • The "Academic Flatlands" Paradox: Human academic processes currently attempt to extract multidimensional, relational, and tacit data from its fluid human state and map it onto structured, two-dimensional "flatlands" (records, screens, and academic scaffolds). This siloed scaffold isolates weak signals before they fade.

Discussion

The migration of data from a fluid, intuitive human plane into a siloed academic scaffold serves a critical systemic purpose: machine optimization. While human intuition thrives on continuous, relational, and embodied contexts, it is highly vulnerable to attrition (burnout, retirement, or memory decay). By flattening this multidimensional data into structured, legible components, academic and technological frameworks build a "memory-native" system. This translation permits AI to act as a continuity infrastructure, preserving weak signals and collective intuition long before formal diagnostic convergence occurs. The ultimate goal is not to achieve algorithmic omniscience, but to establish a system of stewardable uncertainty where machines optimize and scale what humans natively sense.

Keywords

  • Anticipatory Recognition

  • Academic Flatlands

  • Compressed Longitudinal Memory

  • Continuity Infrastructure

  • Human Data Acquisition

  • Machine Optimization

  • Memory-Native Systems

  • Stewardable Uncertainty

Thematic Analysis

Theme 1: Multidimensional Human Data vs. The "Academic Flatlands"

The core tension within human academic and clinical documentation is the transition of data across dimensions. Human experience, clinical intuition, and patient trajectories exist on a "multidimensional plane" characterized by relational nuance, tacit understanding, and unarticulated feelings of concern.

[Fluid Human Plane] ──(Academic Scaffolding)──> [2D Academic Flatlands]
(Multidimensional, Tacit)                       (Siloed, Legible, Machine-Optimizeable)

Academic processes act as an extraction mechanism. They intentionally compress this rich, fluid human data into a two-dimensional "xy axis screen," referred to as the academic flatlands. While this compression strips away some holistic texture, it serves as an essential scaffold that frees data from the temporal limitations of single human carriers, granting it an independent, systemic life.

Theme 2: Intuitive Continuity and Anticipatory Recognition

The transcripts argue that clinical decision-making often operates on an axis of anticipatory recognition—the ability to identify that "something is wrong" long before diagnostic criteria are met or explainable evidence is produced.

"Intuition is knowledge that has not yet learned how to speak."

Rather than being irrational, intuition is operationalized as compressed longitudinal memory internalized within an observer. It thrives on continuous, repeated encounters that build a baseline of familiarity, allowing clinicians and families to detect deviations and weak signals. This intuitive continuity ensures that human stewardship and care can begin before explicit knowledge or formal diagnoses are cemented.

Theme 3: Siloed Scaffolding as a Mechanism for Memory Consolidation

Without structured systems, human memory is highly volatile. The transition of experienced clinicians or the exhaustion of a patient carrier results in a complete loss of institutional and longitudinal wisdom.

Human academic processes provide a siloed scaffold—a structured taxonomy of research questions, case studies, and documentation standards—to intercept these fleeting intuitive insights. By isolating these distributed pieces of clinical memory into structured representations, the scaffold converts fragile human "gut feelings" and loose observations into solid, consolidated records.

Theme 4: Translating Human Wisdom for Machine Optimization

The ultimate objective of flattening and scaffolding multidimensional human data is to make it legible to computational systems. Current artificial intelligence excels at explicit pattern detection but struggles with fluid, tacit context.

By systematically converting human intuition into legible, structured formats, academic processes create an infrastructure that is machine-optimizeable. This enables future AI and digital architectures to:

  • Function as continuous storage units for weak clinical signals that a single human might forget.

  • Externalize collective intuition, transforming a health system from an encounter-based archive into a memory-native system.

  • Optimize the management of stewardable uncertainty, augmenting human judgment rather than replacing it, ensuring that meaning is preserved even when complete data is missing.


How can the design of modern Electronic Health Records (EHRs) be adapted to capture these "weak intuitive signals" without overburdening clinicians with extra documentation steps?

To capture the intricate journey of clinical intuition from the human brain to digital infrastructure, this pictographic analysis visually represents the four core stages discussed in the IMRAD summary. The graphic is structured to show the extraction and formalization of multidimensional human experience into legible, machine-optimizeable data.



Pictographic Journey of Data Transformation




Stage 1: The Human Dimension (Multidimensional Human Data)

This first stage, visualized within the human brain, represents the fluid, organic, and chaotic world of tacit knowledge. Here, the "multidimensional plane" is a network of relational symbols:

  • Intuitive Continuity: This is the foundation where repeated interactions create familiarity. The pictograph uses interweaving flows like "Repeated Observations," "Justified Concern," and "Contextual Relationships."

  • Anticipatory Recognition: A physician icon marks the point where "something is recognized before it is proven." It is operationalized as compressed longitudinal pattern recognition, where clinicians detect weak signals and "gut feelings" long before a diagnosis can be spoken.

Stage 2: The Academic Extraction Process

The transitioning arrows represent the function of human academic and clinical processes: the active "gathering" or "extraction" of this multidimensional, relational data. It is the crucial step of isolating weak signals before they decay or the human carrier burns out.

Stage 3: The Academic Scaffold (Siloed Data Flatlands)

The extraction process flattens the multidimensional human data into the structured, two-dimensional "xy axis screen," also known as the Academic Flatlands. The pictograph visualizes this as a siloed scaffold. Each silo—such as Journey Knowledge, Continuity Stewardship, Stewardship, and Patient Role—is a structured taxonomical bucket where the extracted data is consolidated and solidified into standardized records, folders, and documents. These consolidated memories are now "legible" and "solid," having migrated from a living human carrier into a static, stable systemic archive.

Stage 4: Machine Optimization (Optimizable and Scalable)

The ultimate goal of scaffolding and solidification is realized here. The now-structured and legible "consolidated memories" flow into a digital architecture (represented by binary code and an AI chip). This data is now perfectly machine-optimizeable. The technology can scale the intuition that was once localized to a single clinician or family, allowing the system to:

  • Become a Memory-Native System.

  • Preserve weak signals over vast time spans.

  • Augment Recognition without replacing human judgment, ensuring stewardable uncertainty is optimized and scaled throughout the entire longitudinal journey.

[08/06, 19:35]hu7: As I was working through Case 1 and thinking about the broader architecture of the manuscript, I noticed several secondary questions and lines of inquiry that seem to emerge naturally from the existing RQs.

I do not see these as replacement research questions. Rather, they may be useful as interpretive prompts for discussion sections, future work, or for deepening particular sections if others find them helpful.

They may also create useful hooks for contributors working from different angles: clinical, technological, educational, systems-level, and patient-centered.

In many ways, they feel less like new questions and more like implications of the questions we are already asking.

Journey Knowledge (emerging primarily from RQ1 and RQ2)

If patient journeys are partially observable trajectories and continuity contributes to intelligibility, then additional questions emerge:

* Can a patient be highly visible and still remain unknowable?
* What kinds of knowledge can only emerge longitudinally?
* Are there diseases that cannot be adequately known through episodic medicine?
* Can a trajectory be real before it is clinically legible?
* What is the relationship between recognizability and diagnosability?
* Can healthcare know disease while failing to know the patient?
* Can healthcare know the patient while failing to know the trajectory?

Continuity (expanding RQ2)

If continuity functions as an epistemic instrument, then:

* Does continuity merely preserve information, or can it create new knowledge?
* What observations become meaningful only because other observations survived?
* How much continuity is required before a trajectory becomes intelligible?
* Is continuity a clinical intervention?
* Can continuity alter outcomes before diagnosis changes?
* Does continuity function as a diagnostic amplifier?

Stewardship (emerging from RQ2 and the three temporal cases)

If trajectories require stewardship across time, then:

* What are the stewardship obligations of uncertainty?
* Who owns a trajectory before diagnosis exists?
* Can stewardship failure precede diagnostic failure?
* Is abandonment possible without discharge?
* What is the difference between referral and transfer of stewardship?
* Can ownership be distributed without becoming diluted?

Technology (expanding RQ3)

If technology is to support longitudinal journeys rather than isolated encounters, then:

* What should technology preserve that records currently lose?
* Can AI function as continuity infrastructure?
* What is the difference between storing information and preserving meaning?
* Can a system remember without understanding?
* What would a memory-native health system look like?
* Should healthcare systems learn from trajectories rather than encounters?

Patient Role (emerging from distributed observability and participatory stewardship)

If patients contribute longitudinal knowledge unavailable elsewhere, then:

* When does a patient become continuity infrastructure?
* What forms of epistemic labor do patients perform?
* How much hidden cognitive work is required to remain knowable?
* What happens when the continuity carrier becomes exhausted?
* Can patient-generated synthesis become a legitimate observability artifact?
* How should healthcare respond when the patient becomes the only longitudinal archive?

Recognition (emerging from all three cases)

Across deferred, delayed, and sustained recognition:

* What is the difference between visibility and recognition?
* What is the difference between recognition and action?
* Can recognition occur without ownership?
* Can concern be justified before convergence?
* What survives when recognition fails?
* What is the half-life of recognizability?



[08/06, 23:21]hu5: *Intuition* appears to be the missing layer that sits between *observability, continuity, and recognition*.

What you have already articulated is largely an epistemology of longitudinal care—how healthcare comes to know trajectories over time.

*Intuition* introduces another question:

How does healthcare act before it fully knows?

Or more precisely:

What permits justified concern before diagnostic convergence?

This is important because many clinicians recognize something before they can explain it.

A GP says:

“Something about this patient worries me.”

A nurse says:

“This doesn’t fit.”

A parent says:

“My child is not themselves.”

A CHW says:

“I’ve seen this pattern before.”

At that moment:

* diagnosis may not yet exist;
* evidence may be incomplete;
* trajectories may not yet be legible;
* but concern is already present.

This is where intuition enters.

I would not treat intuition as mysticism or “gut feeling.” Rather, I would define it operationally as:

compressed longitudinal pattern recognition that exceeds explicit articulation.

In other words:

Intuition may be recognizability before explainability.

*Intuition and Recognition*

From your recognition framework emerge questions such as:

* Can concern precede evidence?
* Can recognition occur before explanation?
* Can intuition be legitimate without immediate justification?
* What survives when clinicians cannot yet articulate what they see?
* Is intuition an early form of trajectory recognition?

Perhaps:

Recognition → Explanation → Diagnosis

rather than:

Diagnosis → Recognition.

*Intuition and Continuity*

Without continuity, intuition cannot accumulate.

A single encounter often produces only isolated facts.

Repeated encounters produce:

* familiarity;
* baseline knowledge;
* deviations from baseline;
* weak signals;
* pattern memory.

Perhaps intuition is:

continuity internalized within a human observer.

Questions emerge:

* Does continuity train intuition?
* Can intuition exist without repeated observation?
* Is intuition a form of embodied longitudinal memory?
* What kinds of intuition are impossible in fragmented systems?

*Intuition and Stewardship*

Stewardship often begins before certainty.

Clinicians frequently continue following patients not because they know what is wrong, but because they suspect something is wrong.

Thus:

Stewardship may begin where diagnosis has not yet begun.

Questions:

* Can stewardship be justified by concern alone?
* What obligations arise from persistent uncertainty?
* Can intuition create responsibility?
* When should unexplained concern trigger continued observation?

*Intuition and Patients*

Patients themselves possess intuition.

Parents often recognize illness before objective findings emerge.

Patients frequently say:

“Something is different.”

This raises fascinating questions:

* Can patients possess trajectory intuition unavailable to clinicians?
* Is lived experience a form of distributed pattern recognition?
* Can patients recognize deterioration before systems detect it?
* How should healthcare respond to unexplained but persistent concern?

*Technology and Intuition*

Current AI systems excel at explicit pattern detection.

Human intuition often works on tacit, contextual, and relational information.

Future questions:

* Can AI augment intuition without replacing it?
* Can systems preserve weak signals that humans later recognize?
* Can technology externalize collective intuition?
* What is lost when healthcare privileges explainability over recognizability?

*A Possible New Theme: Anticipatory Recognition*

The three cases you describe (deferred, delayed, sustained recognition) suggest a fourth concept:

*Anticipatory Recognition*

Recognition before convergence.

Recognition before proof.

Recognition before diagnosability.

Not certainty.

Not diagnosis.

But justified concern.

*Perhaps the deepest question* is:

What allows healthcare to care before healthcare can know?

Or even:

Can concern itself be a form of knowledge?

Because many clinicians would say:

“I knew something was wrong long before I could prove it.”

This suggests that intuition may not be opposed to evidence.

Instead:

Observation produces continuity.

Continuity produces recognizability.

Recognizability produces intuition.

Intuition sustains stewardship.

Stewardship eventually enables diagnosis.

So intuition may not be an anomaly within your framework.

It may be one of the mechanisms through which longitudinal systems transform scattered observations into meaningful trajectories.

*In that sense, intuition is neither irrational nor mysterious.*

It may simply be:

*knowledge that has not yet learned how to speak.*

And perhaps the corresponding research questions become:

*Intuition (emerging across RQ1–RQ3)*

* Can recognition precede explanation?
* What forms of knowledge exist before articulation?
* Is intuition compressed longitudinal memory?
* Can concern be epistemically legitimate before diagnostic convergence?
* What role does familiarity play in anticipatory recognition?
* Can intuition be distributed across patients, families, clinicians, and systems?
* Can AI preserve or augment intuition without eliminating human judgment?
* What kinds of trajectories are first recognized intuitively and only later diagnosed formally?

These feel entirely consistent with the architecture you have already built. In fact, I suspect intuition may be the bridge between observability and stewardship. It explains why people continue caring before they fully understand what they are caring for.


[08/06, 23:28]hu5: A thought that came to mind while working through the cases:

We often speak about continuity as something preserved in records, databases, and systems.

But can continuity also reside within people?

Many of us have encountered senior clinicians who seem to recognize something important within minutes of seeing a patient. Perhaps what appears to be “intuition” is actually continuity accumulated over years of experience.

If so, some individuals may themselves function as continuity infrastructure.

This raises interesting questions:

* What kinds of continuity can be externalized into records?
* What kinds of continuity remain embodied within people?
* What happens when experienced individuals retire or leave?
* Can systems preserve information while losing wisdom?
* How should healthcare steward both institutional memory and human memory?

Perhaps continuity does not reside only in charts and technologies, but also in relationships, experience, and people.


[08/06, 23:35]hu5: Perhaps this also explains why ancient textbooks alone are rarely sufficient to recreate a living tradition.

Texts preserve information, but practice also depends on judgment, context, apprenticeship, accumulated experience, and communities of practitioners.

A recipe is not the same as a chef.

Perhaps civilizations inherit knowledge not only through books, but also through living carriers.

The deepest crisis facing any tradition may not be the loss of its texts, but the loss of the people who know how to read them.

As Case 1 evolved, several secondary questions emerged naturally from the existing RQs. These are not intended as additional research questions, but rather as deeper interpretive prompts that may enrich discussion sections, future work, and contributions from different disciplinary perspectives.

RQ1: Observability and Journey Knowledge

If patient journeys are only partially observable trajectories, then several deeper questions arise:

RQ2: Continuity, Stewardship, and Longitudinal Recognition

If continuity functions as an epistemic instrument rather than merely a logistical one, then:

* Does continuity merely preserve information, or can it create new knowledge?
* What observations become meaningful only because previous observations survived?
* How much continuity is required before a trajectory becomes intelligible?
* Is continuity itself a clinical intervention?
* Can continuity alter outcomes before diagnosis changes?

* Is abandonment possible without discharge?
* What is the difference between referral and transfer of stewardship?
* Can ownership be distributed without becoming diluted?

* What allows healthcare to care before healthcare can know?
* Can concern itself constitute a form of knowledge?

⸻

RQ3: Technology, Memory, and Longitudinal Infrastructure

If technology is intended to support trajectories rather than isolated encounters, then:

* What should technology preserve that records currently lose?
* What is the difference between storing information and preserving meaning?
* Can systems remember without understanding?
* What would a memory-native health system look like?
* Should healthcare systems learn from trajectories rather than encounters?
* Can AI function as continuity infrastructure?
* Can AI preserve weak signals before they become diagnostically visible?
* Can AI augment rather than replace human recognition?
* What forms of continuity can be externalized into records and systems?
* What forms of continuity remain embodied within people?
* Can expertise itself be understood as continuity compressed into human experience?
* Are some clinicians themselves living continuity infrastructures?
* Can a patient trajectory ever be fully captured, or are all representations necessarily partial?

⸻

RQ4: Distributed Stewardship, Patient Participation, and Human Memory

If patients and families contribute knowledge unavailable elsewhere, then:

* When does a patient become continuity infrastructure?
* What forms of epistemic labor do patients perform?
* How much hidden cognitive work is required to remain knowable?
* What happens when the continuity carrier becomes exhausted?
* Can patient-generated synthesis become a legitimate observability artifact?
* How should healthcare respond when the patient becomes the only longitudinal archive?
* Can patients possess trajectory knowledge unavailable to clinicians?
* Can families recognize deterioration before systems detect it?
* Can continuity reside not only in records but also in communities and relationships?
* What knowledge survives only through apprenticeship, practice, and lived experience?
* Can a health system preserve information while losing wisdom?

⸻

Cross-Cutting Question: Intuition and Anticipatory Recognition

Across all four RQs lies a recurring phenomenon:

Clinicians, patients, and families sometimes recognize that “something is wrong” before explanation, convergence, or diagnosis exists.

This raises a final set of questions:

* Can recognition precede explanation?
* What forms of knowledge exist before articulation?
* Is intuition compressed longitudinal memory?
* Can concern be epistemically legitimate before diagnostic convergence?
* What role does familiarity play in anticipatory recognition?
* Can intuition be distributed across patients, families, clinicians, and systems?
* What kinds of trajectories are first recognized intuitively and only later diagnosed formally?

These questions suggest that intuition may not represent a departure from observability and continuity, but rather one mechanism through which longitudinal experience becomes recognizable before it becomes explainable.

I suspect these are best viewed not as separate RQs, but as sub-questions that deepen the ontology and epistemology already embedded within the original four RQs. They seem to emerge naturally from the architecture rather than compete with it.


[09/06, 00:04]hu5: A related thought:

Perhaps our expectations themselves need calibration.

If patient journeys are inherently only partially observable, then perhaps the goal of longitudinal care should not be complete knowledge, complete records, or perfect continuity.

Instead, the goal may be sufficient continuity to sustain recognition, stewardship, and care under conditions of unavoidable incompleteness.

In other words, perhaps the expectation should not be omniscience, but stewardable uncertainty.

The patient may always remain larger than the record, and the trajectory larger than its representation.
